svg.text: Same trip, two views: the VPC you configure vs. the hardware that runs it
None of the VPC is physical. Real servers, real cards and real switches pretend to be your private network.
WHAT YOU SEE · the logical VPC (console, Terraform) · 100% software: none of these boxes exist as hardware
↓ dashed lines and matching numbers = "this logical thing is really that physical thing"
WHAT'S REALLY THERE · inside AWS, region us-east-1 (simplified) · solid = physical · dashed = software running on it
AZ us-east-1a = one or more real datacenter buildings
RACK 4 · a metal cabinet of ~40 servers
TOP-OF-RACK SWITCH · every server is cabled here
PHYSICAL HOST A · one real server (CPU, RAM, disks)
VMs + Nitro hypervisor = software sharing this one machine
NITRO CARD · a real network card in the server
Hardware + AWS firmware. Your ENI = its virtual plug.
Your VM can't touch the card, so it can't skip these checks:

text.tspan: security group: is this traffic allowed?

svg.text: the table you configured is enforced HERE

text.tspan: mapping: where does nat-… physically live?
wrap the packet in an envelope and send it

svg.text: outer: host A → node 17 · VPC vpc-0abc…
HOST B · more VMs · its own Nitro card
DATACENTER NETWORK · thousands of switches + fiber
HYPERPLANE · AWS software on a fleet of real servers
runs every NAT gateway, Lambda ENI, TGW, NLB … for all customers
Your nat-… = a slice of this fleet (orange) + the EIP. It isn't one box,
so it scales and survives node failures. Per packet it:
• remembers it in the translation table (for the reply)
• counts the bytes → CloudWatch (the graph we checked)
• then the public route table (0.0.0.0/0 → igw) sends it to the edge
MAPPING SERVICE · the address book of every VPC
VPC + private address → where it physically is

text.tspan: → host A, rack 4 (same IP, other VPC)

svg.text: CONTROL PLANE · where your config lives
You (console / Terraform / API) → AWS stores the config:
route tables, security groups, subnets, NATs …
Seconds later it's pushed to every Nitro card, the mapping
service and Hyperplane (the DATA PLANE), which enforce it
So a route table isn't a device: it's config + enforcement.
lives in one AZ, so you
run one NAT per AZ: if
The same packet at three points of the trip
the Nitro card added the outer envelope
the NAT swapped the inner sender
no envelope, no VPC, no private IP: nothing to attack inward

text.tspan: Customer X's VM on the same host also uses 10.20.33.10. The outer envelope carries the VPC ID, so the network never mixes them up.

svg.text: Simplified from public AWS re:Invent material (Nitro, Hyperplane, the VPC mapping service). Host, rack and node numbers are illustrative.
